title: The British Empire
description: An illustrated world map of how the British Empire grew from a few Atlantic colonies into the largest empire in history, took lands from Spain, the Dutch and France, and then broke up, from 1497 to 1997.
mapLabel: Illustrated world map of the British Empire and its rivals from 1497 to 1997
note: Based on standard histories of the period. The map is stylised and not to scale: it uses a simple flat projection, so lands far from the equator look larger than they are. The empires under Powers are painted loosely on today’s coastlines, with small holdings shown as dots; many borders were vague, or claimed rather than ruled. A few close places (Jamestown and New York, Suez and Jerusalem) have pins that touch. Place names are those of the time. Deaths in wars, camps and partitions are estimates, and historians differ on many of them. Coastlines: Natural Earth.

steps.title: Cabot’s new found land
steps.text: In 1497 John Cabot, a Venetian sailing from Bristol with a licence from King Henry VII, crosses the Atlantic in the Matthew and claims a coast for England. Where he landed is disputed: Newfoundland, Cape Breton Island and Labrador all have claims. Spain and Portugal have already split the new lands between them at Tordesillas (1494).

steps.title: A company for the East
steps.text: On 31 December 1600 Elizabeth I grants a charter to the East India Company, giving London merchants a monopoly of English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope. A Dutch rival, the VOC, follows in 1602 and soon drives the English from the spice islands. The Company turns to India instead; Company, Crown and Freedom tells that story.

steps.title: Jamestown
steps.text: In 1607 about 100 English settlers sent by the Virginia Company found Jamestown, the first lasting English colony in America, on land of the Powhatan people. Most die in the first years from disease and hunger. Tobacco, grown by John Rolfe from about 1612, saves the colony, and in 1619 the first Africans recorded in English Virginia arrive, enslaved.

steps.title: Sugar and slavery
steps.text: English settlers land on Barbados in 1627. From the 1640s planters switch from tobacco to sugar, worked by enslaved Africans shipped across the Atlantic. Sugar makes Barbados England’s richest colony of its time, and its plantation system and harsh slave laws spread to Jamaica and the Carolinas. Before 1700 enslaved Africans far outnumber white settlers on the island.

steps.title: Jamaica, taken from Spain
steps.text: Oliver Cromwell’s ‘Western Design’ aims to seize Spain’s Caribbean empire. His fleet fails to take Hispaniola, then captures lightly defended Jamaica in May 1655. Spain gives up its claim in the Treaty of Madrid (1670). Port Royal becomes a base for privateers such as Henry Morgan, and Jamaica grows into Britain’s largest sugar colony, worked by enslaved Africans.

steps.title: New Amsterdam becomes New York
steps.text: In August 1664 English warships sail into the harbour of New Amsterdam, capital of the Dutch colony of New Netherland. Its governor, Peter Stuyvesant, surrenders without a fight. Charles II gives it to his brother James, Duke of York, and it becomes New York. At the Treaty of Breda (1667) the Dutch keep Suriname, taken from the English.
steps.today: Today: New York City, United States.

steps.title: Gibraltar and the Peace of Utrecht
steps.text: In 1704, during the War of the Spanish Succession, an Anglo-Dutch force captures Gibraltar from Spain. By the treaties of Utrecht (1713), Great Britain, formed by uniting England and Scotland in 1707, keeps Gibraltar and Minorca, gains Newfoundland, Nova Scotia (Acadia) and Hudson Bay from France, and wins the asiento: the right to sell enslaved Africans in Spain’s colonies.
steps.today: Today: Gibraltar, a British Overseas Territory. Spain still claims it.

steps.title: The Atlantic slave trade
steps.text: By the 1700s British ships carry more enslaved Africans across the Atlantic than any other nation’s, from ports such as Bonny in the Niger Delta. Historians estimate British ships carried about 3.2 million people in all, and around half a million died on the crossing; both are estimates from voyage records. Liverpool, Bristol and London grow rich on the trade.

steps.title: From trade to rule in Bengal
steps.text: At Plassey on 23 June 1757 Robert Clive’s East India Company army defeats Siraj ud-Daulah, Nawab of Bengal, after the Nawab’s commander, Mir Jafar, stands aside. In 1765 the Mughal emperor grants the Company the right to collect Bengal’s revenue (diwani). A trading company now governs millions of people. Company, Crown and Freedom tells this story in full.

steps.title: Quebec and the Seven Years’ War
steps.text: In the Seven Years’ War Britain fights France across the world. On 13 September 1759 James Wolfe’s army defeats the Marquis de Montcalm’s on the Plains of Abraham outside Quebec; both generals die of their wounds. By the Treaty of Paris (1763) France gives up Canada to Britain, and Spain gives up Florida. France keeps its rich sugar islands.

steps.title: Cook on the eastern coast
steps.text: In April 1770 James Cook’s ship Endeavour reaches the eastern coast of Australia and lands at a bay he names Botany Bay, where Gweagal men oppose the landing. Sailing north, on 22 August he claims the whole east coast for George III, naming it New South Wales. Aboriginal peoples have lived on the land for at least 50,000 years.
steps.today: Today: Kamay Botany Bay National Park, Sydney, Australia.

steps.title: Yorktown: the colonies break away
steps.text: Taxed by a Parliament where they have no vote, thirteen American colonies rebel in 1775 and declare independence in 1776. France, Spain and the Dutch join against Britain. In October 1781 a British army surrenders to American and French forces at Yorktown, near Jamestown. The Treaty of Paris (1783) recognises the United States; Florida goes back to Spain.

steps.title: The First Fleet
steps.text: Having lost America as a place to send convicts, Britain sends them to New South Wales. The First Fleet’s eleven ships, carrying over 700 convicts plus marines, arrive in January 1788 and settle at Sydney Cove, just north of Botany Bay, on Gadigal land. Smallpox in 1789 and the loss of their land devastate the Aboriginal peoples around Sydney.

steps.title: The Cape, taken from the Dutch
steps.text: When France overruns the Netherlands in 1795, Britain seizes the Dutch Cape Colony to guard the sea route to India, and the next year takes Dutch Ceylon. The Cape is handed back in 1803, then taken again in 1806 and kept. British rule begins over Dutch-speaking settlers, later called Boers, and over the Khoekhoe and Xhosa peoples.

steps.title: Spoils of the wars with France
steps.text: The wars against Revolutionary and Napoleonic France end in 1815 with Britain the leading sea power. At the peace it keeps Malta (taken from the French in 1800), the Cape and Ceylon from the Dutch, Mauritius from France, Trinidad from Spain, and British Guiana from the Dutch. Java, taken from the Dutch in 1811, is handed back.

steps.title: Singapore
steps.text: In February 1819 the Company’s Stamford Raffles signs a treaty with local rulers, the Sultan of Johor and the Temenggong, to set up a trading post at Singapore, at the tip of the Malay peninsula. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 splits the region: Malacca goes to Britain, and the Dutch keep the islands to the south, later Indonesia.

steps.title: Rebellion and abolition
steps.text: After long campaigns by abolitionists, and resistance by enslaved people, Parliament bans the British slave trade in 1807. In Jamaica the ‘Baptist War’ of 1831, led by Samuel Sharpe, is crushed and Sharpe hanged. The Slavery Abolition Act (1833) frees enslaved people from 1834, after unpaid ‘apprenticeship’. Slave owners receive £20 million in compensation; the enslaved receive nothing.
steps.today: Today: Montego Bay, Jamaica, has Sam Sharpe Square.

steps.title: The Treaty of Waitangi
steps.text: On 6 February 1840 William Hobson, for the Crown, and more than 40 Māori chiefs sign a treaty at Waitangi; over 500 sign that year. The English and Māori texts differ: in English the chiefs give up sovereignty; in Māori they grant governance (kāwanatanga) but keep their chieftainship (rangatiratanga). Wars over land follow from 1845 to 1872.
steps.today: Today: Waitangi, Bay of Islands, New Zealand. 6 February is Waitangi Day.

steps.title: Opium and Hong Kong
steps.text: British merchants pay for Chinese tea with opium grown in Company India. When the emperor’s commissioner, Lin Zexu, destroys their opium at Canton in 1839, Britain goes to war. China loses, and by the Treaty of Nanking (1842) gives up Hong Kong Island and opens five ports to British trade. Kowloon (1860) and the leased New Territories (1898) follow.

steps.title: India passes to the Crown
steps.text: In 1857 Indian soldiers of the Company’s army rise in revolt, and the uprising spreads across northern India before it is crushed. In 1858 Parliament ends Company rule, and the Crown governs India directly through a viceroy. In 1877 Queen Victoria is proclaimed Empress of India. India becomes the heart of the empire, with its largest army and market.

steps.title: Canada, the first dominion
steps.text: Plans drawn up at conferences in Charlottetown and Quebec in 1864 lead to the British North America Act. On 1 July 1867 Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick unite as the Dominion of Canada, governing itself at home under the Crown. Other settler colonies follow as dominions: Australia (1901), New Zealand (1907) and South Africa (1910).
steps.today: Today: Canada Day, 1 July, marks Confederation.

steps.title: The Suez Canal and Egypt
steps.text: The Suez Canal, built by a French company with Egyptian labour, opens in 1869 and cuts thousands of miles off the sea route from Britain to India. In 1875 Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli buys the Egyptian ruler’s shares in it. In 1882 British forces defeat an Egyptian army at Tel el-Kebir and occupy Egypt, still nominally Ottoman, for decades.

steps.title: The Berlin Conference
steps.text: European powers meet in Berlin from November 1884 to February 1885 to agree rules for claiming Africa; no Africans are invited. In the ‘Scramble for Africa’ that follows, Britain, France, Germany, Portugal, Belgium’s King Leopold II, Italy and Spain divide almost the whole continent by 1914. Only Ethiopia and Liberia stay independent.

steps.title: Showdown at Fashoda
steps.text: Britain wants a line of lands from the Cape to Cairo; France one across Africa from west to east. In September 1898, after crushing the Mahdists at Omdurman, Herbert Kitchener meets a French force under Jean-Baptiste Marchand at Fashoda on the Nile. France backs down. That same year Spain loses Cuba, Puerto Rico and the Philippines to the United States.

steps.title: The South African War
steps.text: Gold in the Boer republic of the Transvaal draws Britain into war with it and the Orange Free State in 1899. To defeat Boer guerrillas, the British burn farms and hold civilians in camps, where disease kills an estimated 26,000 Boer women and children and at least 14,000 Black Africans; both are disputed. The republics are annexed in 1902.
steps.today: Today: Bloemfontein (Mangaung), Free State, South Africa.

steps.title: The empire at its largest
steps.text: After the First World War the League of Nations hands Germany’s colonies and Ottoman lands to the victors as mandates. Britain takes Tanganyika, Palestine, Transjordan, Iraq and parts of Togoland and Cameroon; its dominions take German South West Africa, New Guinea and Samoa. The empire covers about a quarter of the world’s land, and nearly a quarter of its people.

steps.title: Ireland breaks away
steps.text: Ireland, joined to Britain by the Act of Union (1801), has long resisted British rule. After the Easter Rising in Dublin (1916) and a war of independence, the Anglo-Irish Treaty creates the Irish Free State in 1922, a self-governing dominion. Six northern counties stay in the United Kingdom as Northern Ireland. In 1949 the south becomes a republic.

steps.title: The fall of Singapore
steps.text: In December 1941 Japan attacks British Malaya and Hong Kong, and soon takes Burma and the Dutch East Indies. On 15 February 1942 about 80,000 British, Indian and Australian troops surrender at Singapore, in what Churchill calls the worst disaster in British military history. Many die as prisoners. The defeat breaks the idea that the empire cannot be beaten.

steps.title: India and Pakistan
steps.text: Worn down by the Second World War and faced with India’s freedom movement, Britain leaves India in August 1947, dividing it into India and Pakistan. Partition uproots an estimated 10 to 20 million people, and somewhere between 200,000 and 2 million die in the violence; the figures are disputed. Burma and Ceylon become independent in 1948.
steps.today: Today: Delhi, India. Company, Crown and Freedom tells this story.

steps.title: The end of the Palestine mandate
steps.text: In the Balfour Declaration (1917) Britain backs a ‘national home for the Jewish people’ in Palestine, which it rules under a League of Nations mandate. Arab and Jewish nationalism clash for decades. Britain refers it to the United Nations and leaves on 14 May 1948; Israel declares independence; war follows. An estimated 700,000 Palestinian Arabs flee or are driven out.

steps.title: The Suez Crisis
steps.text: In July 1956 Egypt’s president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, nationalises the Suez Canal. In secret agreement with France and Israel, Britain invades in November. The United States, fearing Soviet gains, forces a ceasefire with financial pressure, and the invaders withdraw. Prime Minister Anthony Eden resigns in January 1957. Britain can no longer act as a great power without American support.

steps.title: Ghana leads the way
steps.text: On 6 March 1957 the Gold Coast becomes independent as Ghana, one of the first colonies in Africa south of the Sahara to win independence. Its leader, Kwame Nkrumah, jailed by the British in 1950, declares: ‘Ghana, your beloved country, is free for ever.’ Malaya follows in August. Ghana’s example inspires independence movements across Africa.

steps.title: The wind of change
steps.text: In February 1960, in a speech to South Africa’s parliament in Cape Town, Prime Minister Harold Macmillan says that ‘the wind of change is blowing through this continent’. That year Nigeria, British Somaliland and Cyprus become independent, and France gives up most of its African colonies too. Apartheid South Africa leaves the Commonwealth in 1961.

steps.title: Kenya and the Emergency
steps.text: From 1952 British forces fight the Mau Mau rising in Kenya, rooted in the loss of Kikuyu land to white settlers. Tens of thousands are held in detention camps, where many are tortured, and over 1,000 are hanged. Official figures count about 11,000 rebels killed; other estimates are far higher. Kenya becomes independent in December 1963, led by Jomo Kenyatta.

steps.title: The Falklands War
steps.text: Britain has held the Falkland Islands since 1833; Argentina, which calls them the Malvinas, claims them. Argentina’s military government invades on 2 April 1982. A British task force retakes the islands, and Argentina surrenders on 14 June. About 650 Argentine and 255 British servicemen die, with three islanders. By now Jamaica, Kenya, Malta, Fiji, Zimbabwe and many more are independent.
steps.today: Today: Stanley, Falkland Islands, a British Overseas Territory. Argentina still claims them.

steps.title: Hong Kong goes back to China
steps.text: As the 99-year lease on the New Territories nears its end, Britain agrees in 1984 to return all of Hong Kong to China. At midnight on 30 June 1997 it passes to China under ‘one country, two systems’, and the last governor, Chris Patten, sails away on the royal yacht Britannia. Many see it as the end of the empire.
steps.today: Today: 14 British Overseas Territories remain, and the Commonwealth has more than 50 member countries.

items.name: John Cabot
items.role: Venetian navigator in English service
items.text: Born in Italy and a citizen of Venice, Cabot moves to England and wins Henry VII’s backing to seek a western route to Asia. His 1497 voyage from Bristol reaches North America. He sets out again in 1498 with five ships; what became of him is unknown.

items.name: Elizabeth I
items.role: Queen of England and Ireland from 1558
items.text: The last Tudor monarch backs privateers such as Francis Drake against Spain, sees off the Spanish Armada in 1588, and in her last years charters the East India Company. Her reign sees England’s first, failed, colonies in America, at Roanoke in the 1580s.

items.name: Oliver Cromwell
items.role: Lord Protector of England, Scotland and Ireland from 1653
items.text: A Parliamentary general in the civil wars that end with Charles I’s execution in 1649, Cromwell leads a brutal conquest of Ireland and then rules as Lord Protector. His ‘Western Design’ against Spain fails at Hispaniola but takes Jamaica in 1655.

items.name: Peter Stuyvesant
items.role: Director-general of New Netherland, 1647 to 1664
items.text: A Dutch West India Company official who lost a leg fighting the Spanish, Stuyvesant governs New Netherland from New Amsterdam. Faced with English warships and a town unwilling to fight, he surrenders in 1664, then lives out his life on his farm on Manhattan, under English rule.

items.name: Robert Clive
items.role: East India Company commander and governor of Bengal
items.text: Clive goes to Madras as a Company clerk and becomes a soldier. His victory at Plassey in 1757 makes the Company the real power in Bengal, and makes him one of the richest men in Britain. Accused in Parliament of corruption, he is cleared in 1773 and dies the next year.

items.name: James Wolfe
items.role: British general
items.text: Wolfe leads the British attack on Quebec in 1759. After weeks of failure he lands his troops by night below the cliffs, and they climb to the Plains of Abraham. He is shot during the battle and dies knowing his army has won. His French opponent, Montcalm, dies the next day.

items.name: James Cook
items.role: Royal Navy captain and explorer
items.text: A Yorkshire farm labourer’s son, Cook rises in the navy as a surveyor. His three Pacific voyages chart New Zealand, Australia’s east coast and much of the Pacific. He is killed in Hawaii in 1779, in a fight with islanders after he tries to take their chief hostage.

items.name: Stamford Raffles
items.role: East India Company official
items.text: Raffles governs Java while Britain holds it from 1811 to 1816, and is sorry to see it handed back to the Dutch. Wanting a British base to rival theirs, he founds a trading post at Singapore in 1819 as a free port. He later helps found London Zoo.

items.name: Samuel Sharpe
items.role: Baptist deacon and leader of the 1831 rising in Jamaica
items.text: An enslaved man who can read, Sharpe plans a peaceful strike for wages after Christmas 1831. It becomes a rising of tens of thousands of enslaved people. Hundreds are killed or executed when it is crushed, and Sharpe is hanged in May 1832. Jamaica names him a National Hero in 1975.

items.name: Queen Victoria
items.role: Queen of the United Kingdom from 1837; Empress of India from 1877
items.text: Victoria reigns for 63 years, longer than any British monarch before her. Cities, lakes and waterfalls across the empire are named after her. She takes the title Empress of India in 1877, though she never visits India. She dies in January 1901, during the war in South Africa.

items.name: Lin Zexu
items.role: Qing imperial commissioner at Canton
items.text: Sent by the Daoguang Emperor to stamp out the opium trade, Lin seizes over 20,000 chests of British opium in 1839 and has it destroyed. He writes to Queen Victoria asking how Britain would feel if opium were sold there. Blamed for the war that follows, he is sent into exile.

items.name: Cecil Rhodes
items.role: Mining magnate and prime minister of the Cape Colony
items.text: Rhodes makes a fortune from South Africa’s diamond mines and dreams of British rule from the Cape to Cairo. His British South Africa Company seizes the lands later named Rhodesia after him. He backs the failed Jameson Raid on the Transvaal in 1895, which helps lead to war. His statues are now contested.

items.name: Winston Churchill
items.role: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, 1940 to 1945 and 1951 to 1955
items.text: As a young war correspondent Churchill is captured by the Boers in 1899 and escapes. Leading Britain through the Second World War, he is determined to keep the empire and fiercely opposes Indian self-rule. He calls the fall of Singapore the worst disaster in British military history.

items.name: Gamal Abdel Nasser
items.role: President of Egypt from 1956
items.text: An army officer who helps overthrow Egypt’s king in 1952, Nasser gets the last British troops out of the Suez Canal Zone by 1956. When the United States and Britain withdraw funding for the Aswan High Dam, he nationalises the canal. Surviving the invasion makes him a hero across the Arab world.

items.name: Kwame Nkrumah
items.role: Prime minister, then president, of Ghana
items.text: Educated in the United States and Britain, Nkrumah returns to the Gold Coast in 1947 and leads strikes and boycotts for ‘self-government now’. His party wins elections in 1951 while he is in prison, and he leads Ghana to independence in 1957. A champion of African unity, he is overthrown in a coup in 1966.

items.name: Harold Macmillan
items.role: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, 1957 to 1963
items.text: Macmillan takes office after the Suez Crisis and speeds up the end of empire in Africa, judging that it cannot be held. His ‘wind of change’ speech in Cape Town in 1960 warns apartheid South Africa that African nationalism cannot be stopped.

items.name: Jomo Kenyatta
items.role: Prime minister, then president, of Kenya
items.text: A Kikuyu nationalist who spends years in Britain, Kenyatta is jailed by the British in 1953 as a leader of Mau Mau, a charge he denies. Released in 1961, he leads Kenya to independence in 1963 and governs it until his death.
